content.text: GENERAL ANESTHETICS & PERIOPERATIVE MEDICATIONS
Mechanism of action of general anesthetics: directly activate GABA-A receptors
Inhalation anesthetics:
Volatile Anesthetics – halothane, isoflurane, desflurane
Gaseous Anesthetics – nitrous oxide
Organ system effects of inhaled anesthetics:
CNS: increased cerebral blood flow
Cardiovascular: decreases MAP & contractility → reduces myocardial oxygen consumption
Respiratory: bronchodilation effects (caution in asthma/COPD), respiratory depression
Nitrous Oxide – clinical uses:
Produce analgesia and amnesia in dental procedures where it may be used alone; when used alone, only Stage II can be achieved, and no skeletal muscle paralysis is achieved

Adjuvant to supplement the actions of other inhaled anesthetics; administering nitrous oxide at inspired concentrations of 50-70% together with another volatile anesthetic decreases the dose requirement of the volatile agent with a reduction of its undesirable side effects
Rapid induction for surgical procedures: poor blood solubility results in rapid tissue uptake
smooth transition from awake to anesthetized state
decreases irritation from volatile agents

Low tissue solubility results in less tissue accumulation during prolonged procedures and rapid elimination from the lungs after d/c; often used to maintain anesthesia near the end of a procedure during elimination of the volatile anesthetic, allowing rapid emergence once surgery is completed
Halothane – clinical uses:
Rapid, smooth induction of anesthesia, especially when administered with 60-70% nitrous oxide
Maintenance of anesthesia in children (commonly used in pediatric practice); infrequently used in adults (replaced by a newer volatile agent after induction is achieved)
WARNINGS: idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity – acute postoperative hepatitis
Desflurane – clinical uses:
Not suitable for induction:  high incidence of respiratory irritation (coughing, breath-holding, apnea, increased secretions, laryngospasms); use IV agent for induction before desflurane anesthesia
Sevoflurane – clinical uses:
One of the most commonly used agents since its introduction
May be used for rapid inhalational induction which is usually well tolerated; nonpungent and lowest amount of airway irritation
Major use is for maintenance
IV Anesthetic Agents:
Used to facilitate rapid induction of anesthesia; have replaced inhalation agents as the preferred method of anesthesia induction in most settings except for pediatric anesthesia
Also commonly used to provide sedation during monitored anesthesia care and for patients in ICU settings
Benzodiazepines – desirable pharmacologic actions:
anterograde amnesia
absence of retrograde amnesia
minimal cardiopulmonary depression
anticonvulsant effects (lorazepam and diazepam are used in treatment of status epilepticus)
relatively safe in overdose due to availability of a specific benzodiazepine antagonist (flumazenil, Romazicon®)
Benzodiazepines – uses:
Preoperative medication: sedation, amnesia
Intravenous conscious sedation
: midazolam
Suppress seizure activity: status epilepticus
Opioids – clinical uses in anesthesia: fentanyl (Sublimaze®), sufentanil (Sufenta®), alfentanil (Alfenta®), remifentanil
Perioperative analgesia
Supplementation of inhaled anesthetics for maintenance
Induction and maintenance:  use of large doses of opioids to achieve general anesthesia in patients undergoing cardiac surgery or major surgery where circulatory reserve is minimal
droperidol/fentanyl (Innovar®, C-II):
Combination of droperidol (Inapsine®), an antipsychotic (
neuroleptic
) agent, and fentanyl (Sublimaze®), an
opiate anesthetic/analgesic
A state of "neuroleptic analgesia" is produced where the patient is psychologically indifferent to the environment and free from pain, but may still be conscious
This is desirable for endoscopic procedures where some degree of patient cooperation is needed
Remifentanil (Ultiva):
Opioid agonist at mu receptors.
Indicated for use as an analgesic agent during induction and maintenance of general anesthesia for inpatient and outpatient procedures
Also indicated for use as an analgesic component of monitored anesthesia care
Etomidate (Amidate)
Short-acting hypnotic; GABA-like effects
Very rapid induction (loss of consciousness in < 30 seconds) and recovery (within 3 min)
Causes minimal CV and respiratory depressant effects (slight hypotension, no change in heart rate, low incidence of apnea)
No analgesia
ADRs: N/V, pain on injection, myoclonus; may also cause adrenocortical suppression
Ketamine
; C-III:
Synthetic nonbarbiturate anesthetic, PCP derivative
Major actions are through inhibition of the NMDA receptor complex
Produces a state of "dissociative anesthesia" characterized by catatonia (sedation, immobility, eyes remain open with a slow nystagmic gaze), amnesia, and analgesia.
The patient feels dissociated and detached from the environment (advantageous for burn dressing changes).
Induction is rapid (loss of consciousness within 30 sec) and analgesia/amnesia is good, but muscle relaxation is poor.
Cardiovascular stimulation is marked and results in increased BP and heart rate.
Recovery is slow and is often marked by disorientation, disturbing dreams, hallucinations, and sensory and perceptual illusions (emergence “delirium” reactions)
IV diazepam given 5 min before ketamine may reduce the incidence of these "emergence" effects.
It may be useful in poor-risk geriatric patients and shock patients because of its cardio stimulatory properties; also used in painful procedures in children.
Propofol
Approved 1989 for induction and maintenance of general anesthesia and in 1993 for sedation of adult patients receiving mechanical ventilation
Used as a component of balanced anesthesia (continuous infusion for maintenance plus an opioid or inhaled agent) and as anesthetic for outpatient procedures (“day surgery”)
Also used for sedation in the ICU as well as conscious sedation and short-duration general anesthesia in locations outside the operating room
Not
approved for sedation in pediatric patients; most serious complication is
propofol infusion syndrome
initially described in children receiving the drug
Dexmedetomidine (Precedex)
Relatively selective alpha-2 receptor agonist; IV sedative
Indications:
for use in ICU to sedate patients who are initially intubated and mechanically ventilated
sedation prior to and/or during surgical or other procedures of nonintubated patients
ADRs: hypotension, bradycardia, nausea
Induction using IV anesthetics:
Propofol – DOC for outpatients undergoing ambulatory surgery
Benzodiazepines
Diazepam and lorazepam are rarely used for induction due to slow onset times, high variability of dose-response, and prolonged residual effects (slow hepatic clearance)
Midazolam has faster onset and may be used for induction in some cases, but its slow elimination usually causes excessively slow recovery and longer cognitive impairment than other agents
Used as a co-induction agent with other IV agents; lessens the CV effects and emergence reactions of ketamine
Use of ketamine or etomidate for induction is restricted to cases where their actions offer advantages over other IV agents
Etomidate can facilitate BP stabilization in patients with severe heart disease or unstable angina
Perioperative Medications
BDZs: produce mild sedation with amnesia; lorazepam
Short- or intermediate-acting barbiturates
Ordered hs before surgery for sedation/sleep
Secobarbital (Seconal®); infrequently used
First-generation antihistamines
Produce sedation as side effect
Promethazine (Phenergan®); also potentiates analgesia
Hydroxyzine (Vistaril®, Atarax®), diphenhydramine (Benadryl®)
Antipsychotics
Side effects:  sedative, anticholinergic, antiemetic effects
Droperidol (Inapsine®), quetiapine (Seroquel®)
Analgesia – preanesthetic analgesia w/ opioid analgesics:
Morphine, meperidine
May decrease amount of general anesthetic required
May prolong recovery, and cause nausea, vomiting, constipation, and urinary retention
Fentanyl transmucosal system
Indicated as a preanesthetic medication in children/adults and for conscious sedation prior to diagnostic or therapeutic procedures
Boxed warning:  risk of hypoventilation, requires close monitoring
Contraindications: children < 15 kg, or for treatment of acute or chronic pain
Antiemetics
Prevention & treatment of postoperative N/V –
ondansetron, granisetron HCl
Droperidol (Inapsine®)
Indicated for prevention and treatment of N/V
Lower doses effective for prophylaxis of N/V than are used for antipsychotic effect; higher doses (> 1.25 mg) cause increased drowsiness
ADR:
sedation
, hypotension; extrapyramidal symptoms rare
Boxed warning:
QT prolongation and production of torsades
; monitor EKG before and 2-3 hrs after administration
Prochlorperazine (Compazine®):
Substantiated effect in treatment of postoperative N/V; less evidence for preventive role
ADR: sedation, extrapyramidal reactions
Metoclopramide (Reglan®):
Unlabeled use for postoperative N/V; relatively weak antiemetic for PONV ; higher doses may be more effective; administer IV over at least 1-2 min near end of surgery
Lower incidence of sedation and extrapyramidal reactions compared to droperidol
Promethazine (Phenergan®):
IV/IM only; SC route contraindicated
effective for prophylaxis and treatment of postoperative N/V
use of promethazine is limited by its sedative action
Scopolamine
Transdermal scopolamine is applied 2-4 hours prior to surgery for prevention of N/V associated with recovery from anesthesia and surgery
ADR: dry mouth, mydriasis, drowsiness; confusion or agitation may occur, especially in older adults with baseline cognitive impairment
Scopolamine patch is contraindicated in patients with angle closure glaucoma
NEUROMUSCULAR BLOCKING AGENTS (NMBAs)
NMBAs – clinical uses:
Perioperative: adjunct to general anesthesia to facilitate endotracheal intubation and to relax skeletal muscle during surgery
NMBAs are never used as substitutes for safe and adequate levels of general anesthesia; NMBAs have no effects on consciousness or pain threshold
ICU: paralysis of mechanically ventilated patients in ICUs; NMBAs are never used in ICUs without adequate sedation and analgesia
Control of muscle spasms associated with certain disease states, e.g., tetanus, status epilepticus
Decrease the muscle activity resulting from ECT
NMBAs – MOA: interfere w/ neurotransmission by:
Occupying and activating the nicotinic receptor for a prolonged period of time, leading to blockade, which occurs with the
depolarizing
agents; or
Competitively antagonizing the actions of ACh at nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, which occurs with the
nondepolarizing
agents.
